newsitem.title: USA: Senate prepares to vote on abortion veto override.
newsitem.headline: Senate prepares to vote on abortion veto override.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday debated whether to override President Bill Clinton's veto of a bill banning certain late-term abortions, with opponents of the measure confident they had the votes to sustain the White House.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, admitted bill supporters were unlikely to prevail, although some senators signalled they would break with the president on the emotional election-year issue.
Vermont Democratic Sen. Patrick Leahy announced he had decided to change his position and vote to override the veto, calling the decision a matter of conscience.
"I have thought and rethought my vote," Leahy said. "On this issue my conscience and my conscience alone must determine my vote and I will vote to override."

The House last week voted 285-137 to override the veto of measure to ban what some people call "partial birth" abortions.The bill passed the Senate last year 54-44, far short of the two-thirds majority needed.

"Partial birth" abortion, technically called intact dilation and evacuation, is sometimes used in second and third trimester abortions. Under the technique a foetus is partially delivered feet first until just the head remains in the birth canal. The brains are suctioned out and skull collapsed.

The legislation marked the first time Congress moved to ban a specific abortion technique. It also represented a turning point in the abortion debate from generalities to a graphic focus on the details of specific procedures.
Republican leaders hoped to use the issue in November elections, painting bill opponents as extremists.

Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole has promised to sign the bill if elected. The Catholic Church has sent 10 million postcards to Congress opposing it and some lawmakers who supported abortion rights in the past voted for the bill.

Bill opponents told heart-wrenching stories of women who discovered late in wanted pregnancies they were carrying horribly deformed foetuses and were told by their doctors the procedure was their safest option.
They charged the bill would endanger women and was a first step toward making all abortions illegal.
"How could we ever know more than a physican?" said California Democrat Barbara Boxer, who spoke next to a large photograph of a woman who underwent the procedure.
"For anyone who thinks this is not in the political arena, why zid it take five months (from the veto) to bring this override here, in the last week of the session?" she said.

The bill has a narrow exception allowing the procedure to save a woman's life. In vetoing the bill, Clinton said he had concerns about the procedure but could not sign it because it did not include constitutional protections for health.
Opponents displayed large black-and-white drawings depicting the procedure, which they compared to infanticide.

"Sometimes party loyalty does demand too much and this is one of these times," said Lott, calling on Democrats to break with the president. "Turning a blind eye to an atrocity is not part of the heritage of the Democratic Party."
There are no accurate statistics on the procedure.
According to the Alan Guttmacher Institute, nearly 90 percent of the 1.5 million U.S. abortions each year take place in the first 12 weeks and only about 600 after 26 weeks.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle said he had promised fellow Democrats to try to work out a compromise next year to ban the procedure for elective abortions, but ensure it would be available in severe medical cases. Abortion opponents called the health exception a loophole to let the abortions continue.
